description: A single unlabelled composite line plot (no micrographs) of the tensile properties of Fe–10Mn–10Al–0.7C low-density steel versus annealing temperature, with the annotation "Time: 1 h". The x-axis runs from the hot-rolled state ("HR", separated from the rest by a break symbol) through 700, 800, 850, 900, 950, 1000, 1100 and 1200 °C. Three vertical axes are used: left red "Strength (MPa)" from 400 to 1200 (ticks every 100); right green "Elongation to Failure (%)" from 0 to 40; right blue "Product of strength and ductility (GPa%)" from 0 to 40. The legend reads: red open squares = Tensile Strength, magenta open squares (dashed) = Yield Strength, green open circles = Ultimate Elongation, blue stars (dashed) = Product of Strength and Ductility. The red tensile-strength marker sits just above the 1100 MPa gridline at HR and falls monotonically to 1200 °C. The magenta yield-strength curve lies just below it and follows the same monotonic decrease. The green ultimate-elongation curve is lowest at HR and 700–800 °C (near/below the 10% line), rises steeply to a peak at 900 °C above the 35% line, then falls. The blue product curve mirrors the green one, peaking at 900 °C just above the 30 mark, so the strength–ductility balance is optimal at 900 °C.

subfigures.description: One unlabelled Cartesian plot with a broken x-axis (HR | 700–1200 °C) and three y-axes (red Strength 400–1200 MPa; green Elongation to Failure 0–40%; blue Product of strength and ductility 0–40 GPa%), carrying four curves: Tensile Strength (red squares), Yield Strength (magenta squares, dashed), Ultimate Elongation (green circles), Product of Strength and Ductility (blue stars, dashed). Note the citing text refers to 'Fig. 16(a)', but the supplied image is a single unlabelled panel.

observations.observation: The supplied Fig. 16 is a single unlabelled line plot with four curves, not a multi-panel figure; the citing text nevertheless refers to 'Fig. 16(a)'.
The x-axis is annealing temperature in °C, plotted at HR (after a break symbol) and then 700, 800, 850, 900, 950, 1000, 1100, 1200 °C, with the in-plot annotation 'Time: 1 h'.

Three vertical axes are present: left red 'Strength (MPa)' from 400 to 1200 in 100-MPa ticks; right green 'Elongation to Failure (%)' from 0 to 40; right blue 'Product of strength and ductility (GPa%)' from 0 to 40.

Legend entries are printed exactly as: 'Tensile Strength' (red open squares), 'Yield Strength' (magenta open squares, dashed), 'Ultimate Elongation' (green open circles), 'Product of Strength and Ductility' (blue stars, dashed).
At the HR condition the tensile-strength marker lies just above the 1100 MPa gridline and the yield-strength marker just above the 1000 MPa gridline, the highest points of both curves.

The red tensile-strength and magenta yield-strength curves decrease monotonically with increasing annealing temperature; at 1200 °C the tensile-strength marker lies between the 600 and 700 MPa gridlines and the yield-strength marker near the 500 MPa gridline.

The green ultimate-elongation curve is lowest in the HR to 800 °C range (markers at or below the 10% line on the green axis), reaches its maximum at 900 °C above the 35% line, and then decreases to 1200 °C.
The blue 'Product of Strength and Ductility' curve follows the green elongation curve in shape and peaks at 900 °C just above the 30 mark on the right-hand axes.
The caption states the figure shows curves of ultimate strength, yield strength, ultimate elongation, and the product of strength and ductility against annealing temperature.

The citing text states that after annealing at 900 °C for 1 h the ultimate strength, yield strength, ultimate elongation and product of strength and ductility are 855 MPa, 651 MPa, 36.6% and 31 GPa%, respectively — these exact values are not printed on the plot itself.
The citing text states that ultimate elongation first increases from 700 °C to 900 °C and then decreases from 900 °C to 1200 °C, and that the change is most violent between 800 °C and 1000 °C.

The citing text states that the change of the product of strength and ductility is mainly decided by the change of ultimate elongation, and that the product reaches its best value at an annealing temperature of 900 °C.

The citing text attributes the high strength but low elongation at 700 °C to continuously distributed κ-carbide along grain boundaries of large α grains, and the drop in strength at 800 °C to κ-carbide coarsening plus better elimination of hot-rolling dislocations.
No numeric data labels are printed on the curves; individual values must be read against the three gridline systems, so only the caption/citation supply exact numbers.

unreadable_items: Exact marker values at each annealing temperature are not printed anywhere on the plot; they can only be estimated from gridlines.

The intermediate x-axis tick labels (between 800 and 900, and between 900 and 1000 °C) are small and slightly blurred at the supplied resolution; the 850 and 950 °C temperatures are inferred from the citation text rather than clearly read.
No panel letter (a)/(b) is visible on the supplied image, although the citing text refers to 'Fig. 16(a)'; it cannot be confirmed whether a second panel exists but was not supplied.
